Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for writing OMIM-style phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited: 100 entries with 2–12 references, 515 papers, 19% readable in full by open access. One model (Claude Opus 5.5) acts as writer, extractor, auditor and judge. The strategies cover three paradigms: read and write (direct reading, an agentic curator), extract then write (an evidence graph, a case table) and memory first (recall, then verify), plus a memory-only control and three add-ons. The primary endpoint is coverage of 6,652 atomic facts. These facts were split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM allelic-variant text deposited in ClinVar about each cited paper, and the model judges each one present, partly present, absent or contradicted. The main findings are as follows. (i) Hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (+43.7 points, 95% CI 38.3–49.1, 46 entries; Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 24). (ii) At the main settings, on the 93 entries every strategy completed, no design conveyed more than direct reading (−0.5 to −1.9 points; Table 1, Fig. 3a). (iii) On 38 held-out entries a completeness pass adds 2.6 points (1.7–3.6) while lengthening drafts by a third. The gain holds on all 41 entries only if the unrevised draft is kept where the safety filter stopped the revision (Sec. 4.3, Tables 30, 32). (iv) A claim-level audit catches citation swaps and moved sentences but not added citations or omissions (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, Table 50). The paper separates pre-specified from post hoc analyses (Sec. 3.3; Tables 2–3) and lists twelve limitations, including that no person validated any judgement (Sec. 5).
Strengths: Clean single-variable design. Entries, sources, model, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed and only the strategy varies (Fig. 1; Secs. 3.2–3.3). Fact lists are fixed once, without sight of any draft (lines 224–226). This avoids the per-draft re-splitting artefact that the paper shows runs 2–5 points higher (Table 6; App. M.4).

The access manipulation is a strong within-paper causal design. The same 91 full-text papers are hidden, the same 2,120 facts are scored, and every arm is unrepaired. Full text is better on 45 entries, worse on 0 and tied on 1, an effect far larger than replicate noise (Sec. 4.1; Table 24). Second-hand passages are measured as a partial substitute (+4.9 points), and passage-based claims are checked against the full text (Table 25).

Statistics and reporting are more disciplined than is typical for LLM pipeline comparisons. The paper gives paired bootstrap intervals, exact sign tests and better/worse/tied counts, with Holm adjustment for secondary measures (Tables 7–8). It adds an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 11), judge-variation and run-to-run replicates with an explicit noise yardstick (App. E, Table 20), and a complete ledger of post hoc choices (Sec. 3.3 lines 259–269; Tables 2–3). The symmetric completion rule for safety-filter stops is a transferable lesson, documented together with the earlier analysis it corrected (App. M.4).

The audit's blind spots are mapped concretely and usefully. Best-verdict aggregation is shown mechanistically to hide over-citation: none of 30 added citations was flagged, although the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' on all 176 claims attributed to it (Sec. 4.5; Table 50). In real multi-citation paragraphs, 4–7% of (claim, cited paper) pairs are non-supporting (Table 53). This is actionable for anyone deploying citation audits.

Contamination is taken seriously. The paper uses a memory-only control broken down by creation era, gene naming from the header alone by era, and 2026 entries held out from all development (Sec. 4.2; Fig. 5; Tables 15–16; App. M.2). It explicitly does not claim that reading is free of memorisation.

Completion, model calls, tokens and list-price cost are reported per strategy (Tables 5, 12, 34). Released pipelines (PaperQA2, GraphRAG, STORM) were tried on the same papers and model, with every deviation from their defaults documented (App. J, Tables 37–39).
Weaknesses: No human validation of any measurement. Fact splitting, present/partial judgements, the 'stated in the supplied text' label, the audit, and the re-examination of draft–reference disagreements all use the same model that writes the drafts (Sec. 3.2 lines 210–214; Limitation (i), lines 509–514). The only reliability evidence is self-consistency (95.7% agreement between two judgings; App. E). The strategy differences behind the comparative claims are 0.5–1.9 points (Table 1), the size most exposed to systematic judge bias or self-preference. For a benchmark whose primary endpoint is model-judged, a curator-labelled sample with chance-corrected agreement is needed to support the claims, even if it covers only a few hundred facts.

Only one model family, and no second writer. The headline conclusions (access dominates; strategies barely differ) may be properties of a frontier long-context model reading short inputs. With a weaker or smaller-context writer, extract-then-write or agentic designs could separate. Limitation (ii) acknowledges this, but no experiment addresses it, so the findings are not shown to generalise beyond this one model.

The regime largely predetermines the null result between strategies. Inputs are small (median 39,450 characters on the padding entries, Table 44), 81% of papers are abstract or title only, and 2,669 of 6,239 compared facts are stated in no supplied text (Table 19; Sec. 5 lines 501–504). When every strategy can read everything, and most facts are either easy to find or not available at all, there is little room for the representation to matter. The tests that could have separated the designs produced no usable comparison. Padding used unrelated papers that no draft cited, leaving 2 entries under the primary rule (Sec. 4.4; App. K.1). Every large entry lost at least one strategy to safety-filter stops (App. K.2). The 30–75-reference tier gives 'no findings' (App. M.1).

The access finding is expected, and its size is partly a property of the reference. The reference is variant-centred allelic-variant text from OMIM gene entries (Sec. 3.1 lines 178–183), whose details (variant notation, zygosity, counts) usually appear only in full text. The supplied text states three quarters of full-text facts but only a quarter of abstract-only facts (Fig. 2b), and the paper itself calls the effect expected (lines 090–091). Without a breakdown by fact type, the 43.7 points mostly says that abstracts lack variant details, not that it is a general bound on agreement with curators.

The endpoint has weak construct validity for 'writing knowledge-base entries'. Strategies write whole phenotype entries but are scored only on per-paper variant facts taken from a different entry type. Only 327 of 515 papers have an in-scope paragraph, and about 24% of a draft's statements have any counterpart in the reference (App. H; Limitation (v)). The endpoint measures recall only (lines 251–252). The reading-better gains therefore cannot be separated from writing more: +2.6 points comes with drafts of 14,412 against 10,802 characters (Sec. 4.3). The only precision-side check is the same model's audit on 20 entries, with no interval (Table 33). The three-draft merge gains partly on facts the text does not state while adding unsupported and contradicted claims (Tables 30, 33), which suggests the judge rewards volume.

Safety-filter stops make the missing entries informative. Comparisons condition on completion, which is itself an outcome of the strategy (Limitation (ii)). For the completeness arms the sign of the mean flips when lost entries count as zero (−3.5 and −4.8; Table 32). The three entries the completeness pass lost are exactly the three where the evidence graph lost a paper (App. I), which points to content-specific triggers that may correlate with entry difficulty. The paper reports this openly, but the headline +2.6 holds only under the keep-the-unrevised-draft convention.

Several analysis choices were made after results were seen, two of which apply to every result. Fixed fact lists replaced per-draft splitting, and the symmetric rule was adopted after a first analysis had put the evidence graph 2.1 points below direct reading (Sec. 3.3 lines 261–264; App. M.4). The main strategies were also developed on their evaluation entries (Limitation (ix)). The disclosure is exemplary, but it reduces the confirmatory weight of the main comparison.

The main comparison is not matched on effort. Writers run at high effort, while per-paper extraction in the extract-then-write strategies runs at medium effort, with synopsis terms assigned by rule (Sec. 3.2 lines 211–214). The matched ablation, which moves the case table by +2.1 points, is post hoc and uses 38 entries chosen for more full text (Table 21). Each paradigm also has a single implementation. The case table's 'suggestive deficit' (−1.9 overall; −8.4 on stated full-text facts, Fig. 3a) therefore describes this implementation at these settings, not the paradigm.

The external baselines are too thin to inform the comparison. PaperQA2 ran without its agent on 10 entries, GraphRAG on 4, and STORM produced no article (Sec. 4.4; Table 35). The six-question, concatenated-answer protocol also differs from one-pass writing, which confounds protocol with design (Limitation (xii)).

Reuse as a benchmark is limited. The curator text and fixed fact lists are not redistributed, so a rebuilt reference must be split again, and the paper did not measure how much levels move under a fresh split by the same procedure (Sec. 3.1 lines 189–193). The writer and judge is a proprietary model called without temperature or seed control. Others therefore cannot score new strategies against the same denominators, which weakens contribution (1).

The presentation is very hard to read. Nearly every sentence in Secs. 1 and 4 carries several numbers, intervals, entry counts and status qualifiers (e.g., lines 093–104, 360–368, 428–431). Readers must keep defined terms ('like for like', 'symmetric rule', 'stopped reply', 'repaired') in mind across sections, and the take-home message is buried. The 45-page appendix with 55 tables documents everything. The main text would gain from fewer, crisper claims, a single summary of effect sizes, and moving secondary numbers to the appendix. Some content is mentioned but not shown: the 'ten approaches reviewed' are never listed (Sec. 4.3 line 412; App. I).
Questions: Can you provide curator or domain-expert labels for a stratified sample, across strategies and access levels, of both the present/partial/absent judgement and the 'stated in the supplied text' judgement, with chance-corrected agreement against the model judge? Do the strategy order and the 0.5–1.9-point gaps survive the observed error rate?

Can a judge from another model family re-score the 93-entry main comparison and the hidden-full-text experiment, to test self-preference and correlated errors between the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements?

Can you break the access effect down by fact type (variant identity or notation, zygosity, counts, phenotype, inheritance, functional evidence)? How much of the 43.7 points is variant detail that abstracts do not contain?

For the completeness pass and the merge, can you give a length-controlled comparison? For example, a direct-reading baseline instructed to write equally long drafts, or coverage per 1,000 characters, together with a precision-side estimate that has an interval and covers more than 20 audited entries.
How much do absolute levels move under a fresh split by the same procedure (same prompt, new calls)? Without that figure, how should external users compare their numbers with yours?

Can the entries and papers stopped by the safety filter be characterised (disease area, content type)? Is completion correlated with entry difficulty or with the other strategies' coverage on the same entries?
Why does the pre-specified main comparison run per-paper extraction at medium effort while writers run at high effort? Would a matched comparison on all 93 entries change the case-table conclusion?
The agentic curator's paper opening is self-reported, and tool calls are not logged (App. B). Can tool use be logged to confirm what it read, and how many read and search calls it made per entry?

In 22 of the 37 facts where a draft contradicted the reference, the same model sided with the draft (App. M.3). Has a person checked any of these? If the reference itself has a non-trivial error rate, how does that change the interpretation of the ceiling?
Is there any pilot evidence on whether a weaker or shorter-context writer, which cannot read everything in one prompt, changes which paradigm comes out ahead?
Limitations: The authors list twelve limitations candidly (Sec. 5 lines 509–535). No experiment addresses the two most consequential ones, the absence of human validation and of a second model family.

The conclusions hold for one proprietary model, small entries (2–12 references), open-access text without supplements, and a variant-centred reference. They should not be read as general statements about LLM-assisted curation or about the relative merit of retrieval, graph or agent designs.
The reference cannot be redistributed and must be split again by anyone who rebuilds it, so results can be compared only as differences within one split, not as levels across studies.
Safety-filter stops make completion depend on the strategy and are not random. They should be treated as a first-class outcome in any claim about deployment.

Drafts of clinical-genetics knowledge-base text may be over-trusted. The ethics statement acknowledges that a passed audit misses over-citation, omissions and copied source errors. The abstract could also state that the 94–97% 'judged supported' rates measure fidelity to the cited text, not correctness.
